children.text: Pan-ay Church (Santa Monica Parish) is a coral-stone church completed in 1884 and declared a National Historical Landmark in 1997 and a National Cultural Treasure in 2004. It is famous for its belfry with a giant bell of about 10 tonnes, called Dakong Lingganay, and lies about 15 minutes by road from Roxas City.

Pan-ay Church is the Santa Monica parish church in the town of Pan-ay, Capiz. The town is one of the oldest settlements on Panay Island, and tradition says Spanish Augustinian friars founded the parish here in 1581. The present building was completed in 1884, with walls about 3 m thick built from white coral-stone blocks. Like other Spanish-era churches in the Philippines, it was built low and massive to withstand typhoons and earthquakes.

What made this church famous among travelers is the giant bell in its belfry. Locals call it "Dakong Lingganay," which means "big bell" in Hiligaynon, and it is said to weigh about 10,400 kg. The story goes that it was cast from coins donated by townspeople, and the bell carries a Spanish inscription saying that it is the voice of God, echoing over the town to call the faithful to church. It is often described as the largest Catholic church bell in Asia, but that claim is disputed, so this guide says only that it is among the largest bells in the Philippines.

The church was declared a National Historical Landmark in 1997 by the National Historical Commission (then the National Historical Institute) and designated a National Cultural Treasure in 2004. The building is a Latin cross about 70~80 m long, about 25 m wide and about 18 m high. Its exterior is plain, but the interior is regarded as the best-preserved church interior on Panay Island. Baroque retablos made by Manila artisans and polychrome statues line the nave and reward a slow look.

As a trip, Pan-ay Church is a short excursion from Roxas City, the base for visiting Capiz. It takes 15~20 minutes from the city center by tricycle or jeepney, and about an hour to see the church, the belfry and the grounds at an easy pace. It is a good stop of an hour in the morning or late afternoon for travelers passing through Capiz on the way between Boracay and Iloilo.

The giant bell hanging at the top of the belfry is said to be about 1.5 m high, about 2 m in diameter and about 10,400 kg in weight. Sources differ on when it was cast, giving either 1878 or 1884. It is rung only on very special occasions, and its sound is said to carry about
8km

The belfry is five storeys high and is climbed by a steel staircase. The stairs are said to number 63, and at the top eight smaller bells hang around the giant bell, with views over the town and the surrounding fields. You need permission from the parish office to climb.

The main entrance is a semicircular arch flanked by niches holding statues of Augustinian saints. The upper level has a niche for St. Monica, a rose window and an undulating pediment, giving a plain but dignified Baroque atmosphere.

The main altar and four side altars hold Baroque retablos carved in silver and hardwood. The floor is terra cotta tile accented with colored marble and black slate, and many of the polychrome statues are said to be the work of local sculptor Jose Bergano.

A full-size replica of the giant bell stands beside the parish buildings. It is said to have been blessed along with the new convent in 2008, and it is a popular photo spot that lets you judge the bell's size even if you cannot climb the belfry.

blocks.title: Lourdes grotto and the old well

children.text: A grotto of Our Lady of Lourdes stands at the foot of the belfry, and the old parish well called "Fuente de Vida" survives on the grounds under a roof. A section of wall behind the church is said to be a remnant of an old fortification.

blocks.title: Historical markers and the bell inscription

children.text: The grounds have a national landmark marker, and a plaque with an English translation of the Spanish inscription on the bell is said to be displayed. Reading it quietly gives a sense of what this bell meant to the people of the town.

items.title: Half day from Roxas City
items.subtitle: Church, belfry and a seafood lunch

children.text: Leave your Roxas City lodging for Pan-ay by tricycle, jeepney or Grab. The ride takes about
15~20 minutes
In the plaza in front of the church, look at the exterior, the facade carvings and the bell replica, and take photos.
Go inside and take your time with the main altar, the side altars, the statues and the floor tiles. Keep quiet during Mass.
Tell the parish office on the right that you would like to visit the belfry, get permission and a guide, and climb the five storeys to see the giant bell and the smaller bells.
Walk the grounds with the Lourdes grotto and the old well, then head back to Roxas.
Have lunch at a restaurant near Baybay Beach in Roxas City, with seafood such as oysters and shrimp.
Belfry access can vary depending on who is working at the office that day. Many visitors report that it is easier to get a guide on weekday mornings.

items.title: A day continuing to Iloilo
items.subtitle: A church trail heading south from Capiz

children.text: Go from Roxas City to Pan-ay Church and spend about an hour looking around.
Take a bus or van south toward Iloilo City. The land route from Roxas to Iloilo is about
116km
Visit Jaro Cathedral and Molo Church in Iloilo City one after the other.
If time remains, stroll the Iloilo River esplanade and stay overnight in Iloilo City.
If you have luggage, you can catch a southbound bus after seeing Pan-ay Church, but flagging buses down along the road depends on local conditions, so using a terminal is recommended.
Domestic flights operate from Manila's Ninoy Aquino International Airport to Roxas Airport (RXS). Airlines and frequencies change by season, so check when you book.
From Roxas Airport, take a taxi or tricycle into Roxas City; the town of Pan-ay lies to the east of the city.
If the schedule does not fit, you can also fly into Iloilo or Kalibo and continue overland.
From Iloilo City to Roxas City it is about
116km
north, taking about
2~3 hours
by road. Buses and vans run; check fares and schedules locally.
The Roxas City Eastern Terminal (Banica) serves routes toward Iloilo, while the Integrated Terminal (Lawaan) serves routes to Aklan and Iloilo.
The town of Pan-ay lies about
7~8km
east of Roxas City, and it takes about
15~20 minutes
by tricycle or jeepney.
A 2012 travel blog reported about ₱150 for a round-trip tricycle from Roxas. The price may have changed, so agree on the fare before you ride.

items.title: By ship and bus from Manila

children.text: Ships are known to run from the Port of Culasi in Roxas City toward Manila, Batangas and Romblon, but routes and schedules change often. Check the shipping line's notices before you go.
Long-distance buses toward Manila (Cubao) also operate from the Roxas Integrated Terminal. The trip is long and suits a relaxed schedule.
In Roxas City, mean daily maximum temperatures are about
and annual rainfall is about 2,137 mm. The wettest months are October (about 305 mm) and June (about 284 mm).

Since you climb the belfry and walk the grounds, it is better to avoid rain. December to May is relatively dry and comfortable for walking, and because the plaza has little shade at midday, mornings and late afternoons are better. Around May 4, the feast day of St. Monica, parish events may be held, so check the schedule.

There are few large lodgings in the town of Pan-ay itself, so most travelers stay in Roxas City and visit as a half-day trip. Roxas is the provincial center of Capiz, with hotels and restaurants concentrated in the Baybay area by the sea. Rates vary by season, so check on a booking site.

Roxas is called the "Seafood Capital of the Philippines," and seafood such as oysters, milkfish and diwal (angel wing clams) is famous. A seafood court near La Playa People's Park is described as serving fresh seafood. After seeing Pan-ay Church, it is convenient to head back to Roxas for lunch.
To climb the belfry, first stop at the parish office to the right of the church, get permission and ask for a guide. Whether it is open depends on who is on duty that day.
The steel stairs are steep, so wear non-slip shoes and hold the handrail firmly.
If you go by tricycle, arranging a round trip with waiting time reduces worry about getting back. Agree on the price and waiting time before leaving.
Many worshippers attend Sunday Mass, so sightsee after the service and stay quiet during Mass.
Avoid sleeveless tops and short pants, and dress with shoulders and knees covered.
The plaza has little shade, so bring a hat, water and sunscreen.
Check Mass times and museum hours locally. Ask at the notice board or the parish office.
The parish phone number is known to be (036) 651-9765, so you can ask in advance about belfry access, but numbers can change, so verify it.
The belfry is not a tourist facility with fixed hours; you climb with the parish office's permission, so it may not be open.
The belfry stairs are steep and narrow, so children and people with weak knees should take care.
This is a place of worship, so take photos without disturbing Mass. Follow the latest rules posted on site.
During typhoon season, conditions at the church and on the roads can change, so check the weather forecast.
The weight and casting year of the giant bell differ by source and are hard to state with certainty. The "largest in Asia" claim is also disputed, so treat it as a reference only.
Taxi or tricycle drivers sometimes quote excessive fares, so agree on the price before you ride.
About
15~20 minutes
west of Pan-ay,
Roxas City
is the center of Capiz, with lodging, seafood restaurants and Baybay Beach.
To the south in Iloilo City,
Jaro Cathedral
is about
2~3 hours
away by road and is a good way to continue a church trail.
Molo Church
in Iloilo City is known for its Gothic style and is usually visited together with Jaro Cathedral.
Miagao Church
, southwest of Iloilo, is a fortress-style church known as a World Heritage Site. It is better to set aside a separate day.
